# 5. Results and discussion

This section reports what the matched meta-stochastic frontier reveals about crop production in households that used credit relative to matched households that did not, and interprets the estimates against the hypotheses of Section 4.1 and the financing environment of Section 3. Section 5.1 presents the diagnostics that justify the frontier specification and the separation of the two groups' technologies. Section 5.2 compares input elasticities and returns to scale across the naive, group and metafrontiers, which speaks to H3. Section 5.3 carries the paper's central result, the decomposition of the credit contrast into a technology gap and a technical-efficiency gap, together with what matching changes and what the matched input and output gaps of Figure 1 add. Because the central result runs against H1, Section 5.4 weighs the readings of it that the data can and cannot support. Section 5.5 tests whether the decomposition survives alternative treatment definitions, matched samples and frontier specifications, and Section 5.6 asks for whom, for which crops and where the gaps are concentrated. Unless stated otherwise, estimates refer to the household credit definition on the one-to-one matched sample, a translog frontier with a half-normal inefficiency term and the regularity restrictions imposed, with jackknife standard errors from 100 delete-one-enumeration-area replicates. Every difference is reported as credit users less non-users, and every difference is an association conditional on observables in a balanced sample, in the sense set out in Section 4.4.

## 5.1 Diagnostic tests

Table 4 reports the diagnostics for the five frontiers estimated: the naive national frontier, the two group frontiers for non-users [A] and credit users [B], and the metafrontier on the matched and unmatched samples. The first question is whether a one-sided inefficiency component belongs in the error at all. The residual-skewness statistics of @Schmidt1984 and @Coelli1995 are negative for every frontier, as a one-sided term in a production frontier implies, the Coelli statistic ranging from `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Coelli (1995)", 3), 2)` for the credit-user frontier to `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Coelli (1995)", 6), 2)` for the unmatched metafrontier, and the boundary likelihood-ratio test of @Gutierrez2001 rejects the null of no inefficiency in each case, with statistics of `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Gutierrez (2001)", 2), 1)` and `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Gutierrez (2001)", 3), 1)` for the non-user and credit-user frontiers and `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Gutierrez (2001)", 5), 1)` for the matched metafrontier. Deviations from the frontier are therefore not attributable to symmetric noise alone, and a stochastic frontier rather than an average-response production function is the appropriate description of the data.

The second question is whether credit users and non-users can be assessed against a single frontier. The metafrontier likelihood-ratio test rejects a common technology in both samples, with statistics of `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Meta frontier LR test", 5), 0)` on the matched sample and `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Meta frontier LR test", 6), 0)` on the unmatched sample, far above any conventional critical value. The two groups produce under different technologies, so their performance has to be decomposed into how well each group uses its own technology and how far that technology sits from best practice, which is what Equations (4) and (5) do; comparing the groups through a single pooled efficiency score would conflate the two, which is the confounding that metafrontier applications to Ghanaian agriculture have been designed to avoid [@Ansah2023a; @Adaku2023; @Asravor2024; @Tsiboe2021a].

The third set of diagnostics concerns regularity and the composition of the error. At the observation level the single frontiers are only partly well behaved: monotonicity holds for `r tbl_pct("table4", "Monotonicity satisfaction rate", 1, 0)` of observations under the naive frontier and for `r tbl_pct("table4", "Monotonicity satisfaction rate", 2, 0)` and `r tbl_pct("table4", "Monotonicity satisfaction rate", 3, 0)` under the non-user and credit-user frontiers, and curvature for only `r tbl_pct("table4", "Curvature satisfaction rate", 1, 0)`, `r tbl_pct("table4", "Curvature satisfaction rate", 2, 0)` and `r tbl_pct("table4", "Curvature satisfaction rate", 3, 0)` respectively, although every elasticity is positive at the sample means at which it is evaluated, so the models are well behaved on average even where individual observations violate the conditions. The regularity-restricted metafrontier does what it is meant to do: monotonicity is satisfied for `r tbl_pct("table4", "Monotonicity satisfaction rate", 5, 0)` of observations in both the matched and the unmatched metafrontier, and curvature for `r tbl_pct("table4", "Curvature satisfaction rate", 5, 0)` of observations in the matched metafrontier against `r tbl_pct("table4", "Curvature satisfaction rate", 6, 0)` in the unmatched one. The matched metafrontier is therefore the specification on which the elasticities and technology gaps below can be read with the least concern about local violations of economic regularity, which is one reason, alongside covariate balance, for treating the matched estimates as the preferred ones. The share of composed-error variance attributable to the one-sided term, $\gamma = \sigma_{u}^{2}/\sigma^{2}$, is `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Ratio variance due to inefficiency", 2), 3)` in the non-user frontier and `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Ratio variance due to inefficiency", 3), 3)` in the credit-user frontier, so within each group the dominant source of unexplained dispersion is inefficiency rather than noise; in the metafrontier, where the one-sided term is the technology gap, the share is `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Ratio variance due to inefficiency", 5), 3)` on the matched sample against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Ratio variance due to inefficiency", 6), 3)` on the unmatched one, so most of the distance between the group frontiers and the envelope is systematic rather than idiosyncratic. Both margins matter, which is the premise on which the metafrontier design rests.

## 5.2 Output elasticities and returns to scale

Table 4 reports input elasticities evaluated at the sample means, with the underlying translog coefficients in Table S3. Under the naive national frontier every input has a positive elasticity that is significant at the 1% level, consistent with earlier frontier estimates for Ghanaian crop production on these data [@Tsiboe2021a; @Ansah2023a; @Adaku2023; @Asravor2024]. Land dominates, with an elasticity of `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Land", 1), 3)`, followed by family labour (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Family labour", 1), 3)`), planting material (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Planting material", 1), 3)`), pesticide (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Pesticide", 1), 3)`), hired labour (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Hired labour", 1), 3)`) and fertilizer (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Fertilizer", 1), 3)`). Returns to scale are `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Returns to scale", 1), 3)`, marginally above constant. The ordering is the familiar one for Ghanaian smallholders, whose output responds overwhelmingly to the extensive margin and to household labour and only modestly to purchased inputs.

The group frontiers speak to H3, and the evidence is narrower than the hypothesis anticipated. Because the jackknife standard errors are small, most differences in the [B−A] column are statistically significant, and it is their magnitude that carries the economic content. On that criterion one input stands out. The family-labour elasticity is `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Family labour", 3), 3)` for credit users against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Family labour", 2), 3)` for non-users, a difference of `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Family labour", 4), 3)` that is significant at the 1% level, about a third of the non-user elasticity, and accounts for almost the whole of the returns-to-scale gap (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Returns to scale", 3), 3)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Returns to scale", 2), 3)`, a difference of `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Returns to scale", 4), 3)`). The land elasticity is identical across groups to three decimals (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Land", 2), 3)` and `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Land", 3), 3)`), so credit is not associated with higher returns at the extensive margin. The fertilizer elasticity is slightly higher for credit users (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Fertilizer", 3), 3)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Fertilizer", 2), 3)`), which runs opposite to the sign H3 posited, hired labour is higher by `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Hired labour", 4), 3)`, and planting material and pesticide are lower by `r fmt_num(abs(tbl_num("table4", "Planting material", 4)), 3)` and `r fmt_num(abs(tbl_num("table4", "Pesticide", 4)), 3)`; each of these differences is below one percentage point of output and none would change the ranking of inputs within either group. H3 is thus supported for family labour and not for land, and the fertilizer elasticity moves in the wrong direction by an amount too small to bear interpretation, from a base that is small for both groups. That fertilizer margin is worth a further word, because a leading account of low fertilizer use in African agriculture attributes it to uninsured risk acting together with the absence of credit rather than to either alone: in Ethiopia, households more exposed to a shortfall in consumption after a bad harvest applied less fertilizer, so that risk and the inability to borrow against the outlay reinforced one another [@Dercon2011]. If that account carried over to the population studied here, households whose credit constraint is the less binding of the two would show a distinctly different fertilizer regime from comparable non-borrowers. They do not. The two group frontiers differ on fertilizer by an amount too small to interpret, the higher of the two elasticities being the credit users' rather than the non-users', and the quantity of fertilizer actually applied, taken up with Figure 1 in Section 5.3, is lower among borrowers than among their matched comparators. Neither margin is what that account would predict, so the Ethiopian evidence stands as a contrast to what these data show rather than a confirmation of it, and the contrast is one more reason to ask, as Section 5.4 does, whether the borrowing recorded here is the kind that finances fertilizer at all. The credit-user technology is not more input-responsive across the board; it is more responsive to household labour, at the same returns to land and with mildly increasing rather than constant returns to scale.

Two readings of the family-labour result are consistent with the data, and the design cannot separate them. One is that credit-using households deploy their own labour more productively at the margin, for instance through better timing of operations that liquidity makes possible; an elasticity describes the curvature of a group's frontier at its mean input bundle, so a higher family-labour elasticity is consistent with those farms operating where additional household labour still adds substantially to output, particularly if, as Figure 1 shows below, they combine it with fewer purchased inputs. The other is compositional: the group frontier is fitted on the borrowing households as they are, and a frontier fitted on a younger, more educated group can display a higher family-labour elasticity without any change in how a given household farms. Table S3 adds one feature worth carrying forward to the heterogeneity results. The coefficient on the cocoa area share is positive in every frontier and much larger in the credit-user frontier (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("tableS3", "Cocoa", 3), 3)`) than in the non-user frontier (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("tableS3", "Cocoa", 2), 3)`), so the technology credit users operate is relatively favourable to cocoa even though, as shown below, it is less favourable to most other crops.

The last two columns of Table 4 give the metafrontier elasticities on the matched and unmatched samples. The two are close and preserve the same ranking of inputs: land is `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Land", 5), 3)` matched against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Land", 6), 3)` unmatched, family labour `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Family labour", 5), 3)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Family labour", 6), 3)`, planting material `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Planting material", 5), 3)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Planting material", 6), 3)`, pesticide `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Pesticide", 5), 3)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Pesticide", 6), 3)`, and returns to scale `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Returns to scale", 5), 3)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Returns to scale", 6), 3)`, with hired labour and fertilizer coinciding to within a thousandth. Balancing the sample therefore changes the shape of the envelope only modestly; its main effect, shown next, is on the position of the two groups relative to it. What the elasticities establish is that the best-practice technology, like both group technologies, is land-intensive with near-constant returns to scale, so the technology gaps discussed next are gaps in the level of the frontier rather than in its shape.

## 5.3 Technology gaps, technical efficiency and meta-frontier efficiency

Table 4 decomposes performance into the technology gap ratio of Equation (4), pure technical efficiency from Equation (2) and their product, meta-frontier technical efficiency, from Equation (5); the Matched rows are the preferred estimates and the Unmatched rows show what balancing the sample changes. Table 5 repeats the matched comparison for the household definition alongside the narrower definitions of who in the household borrowed, which Section 5.5 takes up.

The technology gap is the headline result, and it runs against H1. In the matched sample the mean TGR is `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 2, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)"), 3)` for non-users and `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 3, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)"), 3)` for credit users: the technology set operated by non-users produces, on average, `r fmt_pct(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 2, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)"), 0)` of the output attainable under the best-practice technology at the same inputs, and that of credit users `r fmt_pct(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 3, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)"), 0)`. The difference of `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 4, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)")), 1)` percentage points is significant at the 1% level, is reproduced exactly in the first row of Table 5, and is negative. Section 4.1 hypothesized the opposite on the grounds that credit finances the lumpy investments that move a farm toward best practice. In these data borrowing households are not, as a group, operating the best-practice technology; their frontier lies farther inside the metafrontier than the frontier of comparable non-users, and matching on gender, round, region, agro-ecology, locality and a rich set of household, farm and financial-inclusion covariates does not remove that difference. The unmatched gap is of the same sign and similar size (`r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table4", "Unmatched", 4, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)")), 1)` percentage points), so the finding is not created by matching either.

Pure technical efficiency, which measures each group against its own frontier, differs little between the groups, and the sign of the small difference is not stable across specifications. Table 4, built from the regularity-restricted frontiers, gives mean TE of `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 2, block = "Pure farmer technical efficiency (TE)"), 3)` for non-users and `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 3, block = "Pure farmer technical efficiency (TE)"), 3)` for credit users, a difference of `r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 4, block = "Pure farmer technical efficiency (TE)"), 1)` percentage points in favour of credit users; Table 5, built from the unrestricted frontiers, gives `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table5", "Anyone including farmer", 1, block = "Pure farmer technical efficiency (TE)"), 3)` and `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table5", "Anyone including farmer", 2, block = "Pure farmer technical efficiency (TE)"), 3)` for the same definition, a difference of `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table5", "Anyone including farmer", 3, block = "Pure farmer technical efficiency (TE)")), 1)` points against them, and Section 5.5 shows that the sign also moves across matched samples and aggregation rules. Both differences are statistically significant because the jackknife standard errors are small, but a gap that changes sign with the regularity restrictions imposed on the frontier, and that stays within about two percentage points of zero under every specification examined, is not a gap on which an interpretation should rest. The defensible statement is that, relative to their own technology, credit users and matched non-users are about equally efficient, each attaining roughly `r fmt_pct(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 2, block = "Pure farmer technical efficiency (TE)"), 0)` of their own frontier output, a level of within-technology inefficiency in line with earlier Ghanaian frontier studies [@Ansah2023a; @Asravor2024; @Adaku2023]. H2, which predicted lower efficiency among credit users, receives at most weak support, and we do not read the data as establishing an efficiency penalty of borrowing.

Because the efficiency margin is close to neutral, the meta-frontier efficiency gap is the technology gap. Matched MTE is `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 2, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)"), 3)` for non-users and `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 3, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)"), 3)` for credit users in Table 4, a statistically significant shortfall of `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 4, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)")), 1)` percentage points, and `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table5", "Anyone including farmer", 1, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)"), 3)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table5", "Anyone including farmer", 2, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)"), 3)` in Table 5, a shortfall of `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table5", "Anyone including farmer", 3, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)")), 1)` points. Whichever specification is preferred, the MTE gap is negative, significant and of the same order as the TGR gap, so the shortfall of credit-using households relative to best practice is a technology gap and not an efficiency gap. Both groups, it should be stressed, operate well inside the metafrontier, at about `r fmt_pct(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 2, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)"), 0)` and `r fmt_pct(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 3, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)"), 0)` of attainable output; the credit gap is a modest increment on a large common shortfall of the kind widely documented for African smallholders [@Ogundari2014; @Ansah2023a], and the economically relevant statement is not that borrowers farm worse but that the technology they farm with is, on average, farther from the best available, by an amount several times the efficiency difference in either direction. The attribution differs from the one @Ansah2023a report across agro-ecologies, where technical inefficiency outweighs technology differences. The two results are not in conflict, because they decompose different contrasts, but together they caution against assuming that any production shortfall in Ghana is a management problem.

The comparison between the matched and unmatched rows of Table 4 shows what matching does to these contrasts, and it is the most informative feature of the table. In the unmatched sample credit users trail non-users by `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table4", "Unmatched", 4, block = "Pure farmer technical efficiency (TE)")), 1)` percentage points in TE and `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table4", "Unmatched", 4, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)")), 1)` points in MTE, several times the matched values, whereas the unmatched TGR gap is close to the matched one. Balancing the two groups on observables therefore removes almost all of the raw efficiency disadvantage of borrowers and most of the raw MTE deficit, but leaves the technology gap essentially intact. The raw efficiency deficit was compositional, a statement about who borrows on the dimensions Section 4.3 balances; the technology gap survives the comparison of like with like. Observable selection into borrowing explains the efficiency difference and almost none of the technology difference.

Figure 1 places the frontier results beside the input and output levels of the matched pairs. It reports, for the matched sample, the proportional gap associated with credit in each per-hectare input and in the real value of output per hectare, evaluated for the sample as a whole and with reference to the non-user and user subsamples. Credit-using households apply substantially less fertilizer, planting material, hired labour and pesticide per hectare than their matched comparators, the fertilizer gap being the largest and each of the four gaps significant at the 1% level; land area, against which the other inputs are normalized, registers no gap; household labour does not differ significantly; and the value of output per hectare is slightly higher for credit users, a difference that does not reach the 5% level. The three reference populations give nearly identical gaps, so the pattern does not depend on which group's covariate distribution is used. Two things follow. First, the hired-labour advantage of borrowing households in the unmatched data of Table 1 (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("table1", "Hired labour (man-days/ha)", 3), 0)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table1", "Hired labour (man-days/ha)", 2), 0)` man-days per hectare) does not survive comparison with observably similar non-borrowers; it reflected who borrows rather than what borrowing finances. Second, credit is not associated with intensification on the purchased-input margin in these data, which is the opposite of what a liquidity-relaxing account of credit predicts. Read with Table 4, the picture is of a borrowing group whose technology relies more on land and household labour and less on purchased inputs, lies inside the best-practice envelope, produces about as much per hectare as the comparison group, and is run about as efficiently, relative to that technology, as the comparison group runs its own. The lower TGR of credit users therefore cannot be read as borrowed money buying inputs that fail to raise output; it is the technology in use, evaluated at common input levels, that sits farther from best practice.

## 5.4 Interpreting the negative technology gap

The technology gap is measured against a metafrontier that envelops both group frontiers, so a lower TGR for credit users says that the technology of borrowing households, as a group, is not the best practice in the sample. It does not say what makes it so, and Section 4.4 rules out a causal reading. Four readings are consistent with the evidence of Sections 2, 3 and 5.3, and the data discriminate among them only partially.

The first is loan use. Household credit relaxes the household's liquidity constraint, not the farm's, and the loan-purpose codes of Table 3 show that agriculture is a minority use of it: in 2012/13, the round in which the recorded purposes exhaust the loans, only `r tbl_pct("table3", "Agricultural", 1, 1)` were taken for agricultural purposes, the remainder financing business, education, ceremonies, debt repayment and other household needs. Fungibility of agricultural credit within the household is well documented [@Hussain2016], and Figure 1 is what fungibility looks like on the farm: borrowing households are not the ones applying more purchased inputs. On this reading the negative technology gap is not a failure of credit to reach the farm so much as evidence that, for most of these households, the loan was never directed there, and the household indicator identifies households with a reason to borrow rather than farms with financed technology. This is the reading the exhibits most directly support, and it is consistent with the northern-Ghana finding that even input-linked credit raised input use without proportionate output gains [@Iddrisu2018]; the survey records the stated purpose of a loan but not the use of each cedi, so it cannot be confirmed at the level of the individual farm.

The second is selection on what the GLSS does not record. Matching balances the covariates in Table 1 and Fig. S1, but not the reasons a household applies for a loan and a lender grants it. Distress borrowing after a shock, borrowing to fund a non-farm enterprise, and lender targeting of households with particular repayment prospects would each place borrowers on a different technology for reasons the design cannot see, and the growing share of group-based microfinance in Table 3, from `r tbl_pct("table3", "Group based micro-finance or lending", 1, 1)` to `r tbl_pct("table3", "Group based micro-finance or lending", 2, 1)` of loans, means that allocation increasingly runs through community institutions whose membership the GLSS does not observe. Differences in risk preference that affect both borrowing and technology choice belong here too [@Dercon2011]. The stability of the TGR gap between the unmatched and matched samples is consistent with this reading, since it shows that the gap is orthogonal to the observables the matching uses; it cannot show whether the gap is orthogonal to what the matching does not use, and the direction of the resulting bias is not signed.

The third is the distinction between use and access. The treatment is an indicator of having borrowed, and the modal reason for not applying is having no need for a loan (`r tbl_pct("table3", "No need", 1, 1)` and `r tbl_pct("table3", "No need", 2, 1)` of non-applicants in the two rounds, Table 3), so the comparison group mixes households that are credit constrained with a larger number that, on their own account, are not. The literature that finds credit constraints lowering farm productivity identifies the constrained explicitly [@Guirkinger2008; @Kumar2013; @Dessie2015]; the contrast estimated here is a different object, and a negative gap for borrowers against a largely unconstrained comparison group is not in tension with it. If the households that choose not to borrow are, on average, the ones already operating the better technology, the estimated gap partly reflects that sorting. Table 6 offers a partial check. Within households in which the operator applied for a loan, a subgroup in which demand is held constant, the TGR contrast between credit users and applicants whose household did not obtain credit is `r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Loan applied", 1), 1)` percentage points, close to the full-sample gap, so the headline gap is not an artefact of comparing applicants with non-applicants; the TE and MTE contrasts in that row are larger, but the unfunded comparison group is small and is selected by lenders' decisions, so we do not lean on them. Experimental evidence from Ghana approaches the same distinction from the supply side. Offering maize farmers in the north rainfall-index insurance and cash grants in varying combinations, @Karlan2014 find that farm investment responded to the relaxation of the risk constraint and changed little when capital alone was supplied, which places the binding constraint for that population in uninsured risk rather than in liquidity. On that evidence a negative technology gap among borrowers is not in itself surprising, because relaxing a credit constraint need not move a farm's technology when risk is what binds, and the near-absence of cover against production risk documented in Section 3 is part of the environment in which the loans observed here were taken. The experiment does not, however, settle the reading of the contrast estimated here: it supplied capital to farmers who did not have to seek it, in one crop and one region, so it speaks to access where this treatment records use, and it identifies which constraint binds where this design can only describe the households in which borrowing is observed.

The fourth is measurement. Section 4.3 argues that self-reported borrowing under-records small and informal loans, which would place some genuine borrowers in the comparison group and attenuate the contrast toward zero. Attenuation does not generate a negative gap; it makes the estimated gap, if anything, an understatement of the true difference in absolute value. It cannot explain the sign.

What the data cannot do is assign weights to these readings. The GLSS records the purpose of a loan but not what the household did with the liquidity it freed, records that a loan was granted but not why, and records use rather than access. The disaggregations of Section 5.6 narrow the space somewhat, because the technology gap is present in every financial-service subgroup and every region, which is difficult to reconcile with a story confined to one lending channel or one agro-ecology. The honest summary is that the negative technology gap is a robust description of Ghanaian borrowing households, not an estimate of what credit does to a farm.

Placed against the Ghanaian literature, the result reconciles rather than contradicts. Positive credit-efficiency associations have been reported for maize producers under programme and input-linked financing [@Martey2019; @AppiahTwumasi2022], no association for rice under bank-linked credit [@Anang2016], modest output effects of input credit [@Iddrisu2018], and financial inclusion more broadly has been linked to smallholder productivity [@Peprah2021]. Those studies observe credit tied to farm inputs, or crops and regions in which such credit predominates, and they compare borrowers and non-borrowers on a single frontier; the estimates here are national in scope, net of matching on observables, and drawn from a population in which little household borrowing is agricultural. The nationally representative decomposition therefore does not show that agricultural credit fails to move farms toward the frontier; it shows that credit as households actually obtain and use it is not associated with best-practice technology and does not raise or lower within-technology efficiency in any robust way. The distinction between agricultural credit and credit in agricultural households is the paper's substantive contribution to that literature.

Table S4 adds covariate detail that points the same way. In the matched metafrontier, whose one-sided term is the technology gap, the gap is larger for female-operated farms (coefficient `r fmt_num(tbl_num("tableS4", "Female farmer (dummy)", 4), 3)`) and smaller where the household owns its land (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("tableS4", "Land owned (dummy)", 4), 3)`), uses mechanized equipment (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("tableS4", "Mechanization (dummy)", 4), 3)`), receives extension advice (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("tableS4", "Extension (dummy)", 4), 3)`) or grows a more diversified crop mix (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("tableS4", "Crop diversification (index)", 4), 3)`), all significant at the 1% level, while years of schooling carries a small positive coefficient (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("tableS4", "Education (years)", 4), 3)`), meaning a larger distance from best practice. Distance from best practice is thus associated with the same tenure, service and gender factors that structure technology access in Ghanaian agriculture generally [@Adaku2023; @Asravor2024], not with the borrowing indicator that defines the groups.

The policy reading follows from which channel carries the gap. A shortfall located in technical efficiency would call for managerial support through extension, training and record-keeping bundled with the loan; the evidence does not support that diagnosis, because the efficiency difference is small, of unstable sign, and disappears once borrowers are compared with similar non-borrowers. A shortfall located in the technology gap calls for changing the technology farms can obtain and use, but here the gap is not the technology gap that input-constrained farms display, because credit users apply fewer purchased inputs rather than more, and it appears alongside loans that are mostly not used on the farm. The finding therefore does not support expanding household credit as such as an instrument for closing Ghana's crop technology gap, and it does not support the opposite proposition either, since the design cannot establish what credit does to a given farm. It is consistent with the view, long argued for agricultural finance in sub-Saharan Africa, that finance moves technology only when it is designed around the farm's investment and timing needs and bundled with the inputs, information and risk instruments that make the investment worth undertaking [@Meyer2015; @Barrett2022], and with demand-side accounts in which low uptake reflects the limited value farmers see in the products on offer [@DeJanvry2020]. The bundling argument is consistent with these findings, but it is not tested by them; Section 6 draws out the implications after the robustness and heterogeneity evidence has been presented.

## 5.5 Robustness of the main findings

Three features of the main result need to survive scrutiny: the sign and size of the TGR gap, the smallness of the TE gap, and the consequent attribution of the MTE gap to technology. Efficiency scores are not specification-free. The inputs entered, the functional form, the distribution assumed for the one-sided term and the estimator used to recover producer-level scores can each move mean efficiency and the ranking of producers within the same data [@VanNguyen2021], so no single specification can establish the size, and still less the sign, of a difference between two groups' scores; the spread of estimates across defensible specifications is itself the evidence, and we read it that way rather than selecting the specification that gives the cleanest answer. We examine each of the three features across the definition of treatment, the matched sample and the frontier specification, and the exercise separates them rather than confirming them together: the technology component holds its sign and its size throughout, while the efficiency component does not.

Table 5 varies whose borrowing defines the household as a credit user; each definition is fitted as its own pair of frontiers, so the non-user column varies across rows. The technology gap is negative and significant at the 1% level under every definition, and larger under the narrower ones: `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table5", "Anyone including farmer", 3, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)")), 1)` percentage points for household credit, `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table5", "Farmer", 3, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)")), 1)` points for the operator's own credit, `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table5", "Spouse of farmer", 3, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)")), 1)` points for spousal credit and `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table5", "Household members other than spouses or child", 3, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)")), 1)` points for credit held by another member. The household definition, being the broadest, gives the smallest gap, so the preferred estimate is if anything the conservative one, and the operator-only definition promised in Section 2.2 reproduces the headline result with a larger magnitude. The TE difference is small under every definition but not of one sign: it runs against credit users by `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table5", "Farmer", 3, block = "Pure farmer technical efficiency (TE)")), 1)` points under the operator-only definition and by `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table5", "Household members other than spouses or child", 3, block = "Pure farmer technical efficiency (TE)")), 1)` points under the other-member definition, but in their favour, by `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table5", "Spouse of farmer", 3, block = "Pure farmer technical efficiency (TE)")), 1)` points, when the spouse holds the loan. The MTE gap is negative throughout, from `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table5", "Spouse of farmer", 3, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)")), 1)` points under spousal credit to `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table5", "Farmer", 3, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)")), 1)` points under the operator-only definition, and in each case the technology gap is the larger component. Whose borrowing is counted changes the size of the shortfall and the sign of its small efficiency component; it does not change the direction of the technology gap or of overall performance, and a contrast that holds for the operator's own loan, a spouse's loan and another member's loan is harder to attribute to operator-specific unobservables.

Fig. S1 reports covariate balance for the unmatched sample and for each of the eight matched samples described in Section 4.3, on absolute standardized mean differences, variance ratios and Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics. The unmatched sample is most imbalanced on schooling, household size and several crop-share, ethnicity and regional indicators. Every matched sample brings the standardized differences and Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics close to zero on nearly all covariates, the propensity-score and robust Mahalanobis schemes bring the variance ratios closest to one, and the differences among the propensity-score schemes are small, so the choice among them is not consequential for balance; the probit propensity-score sample, which the composite ranking selects, underlies Tables 4 to 6 and Figures 1 to 4. Two covariates deserve mention. Household size is the one covariate on which a standardized difference of moderate size survives in every matched sample, and the propensity-score matches leave a moderate difference in operator age that the distance-based matches remove, so balance on those dimensions is imperfect; given the family-labour result of Section 5.2, this is a further reason not to over-read the small TE gap.

Fig. S2 re-estimates the three gaps under the alternative specifications listed in Section 4.5, with the preferred estimate marked as a reference band. Across the eight matched samples, formed on Euclidean, scaled Euclidean, Mahalanobis and robust Mahalanobis distance and on logit, probit, complementary log-log and cauchit propensity scores, the TGR gap is negative and of similar size in every case, the MTE gap is negative in every case, and the TE gap moves on both sides of zero within a narrow band. The unmatched sample stands apart with a far larger negative TE and MTE gap and a TGR gap close to the matched ones, which repeats the lesson of Table 4. Replacing the translog with a Cobb-Douglas frontier, computing scores by the Jondrow-type or the conditional-model estimator rather than the Battese-Coelli estimator, and aggregating operator-level scores by the simple mean or the median rather than the weighted mean all leave the TGR and MTE gaps negative and close to the preferred estimate, while the TE gap again changes sign across these choices. Lifting the regularity restrictions leaves the TGR gap identical and moves only the TE and MTE gaps, both of which become more negative under the unrestricted frontier; this is the same restricted-against-unrestricted difference that separates Table 4 from Table 5, and it is why the paper treats the TGR gap as the robust finding and the sign of the TE gap as unresolved.

The distributional checks are the least reassuring and deserve to be stated plainly. The exponential distribution for the one-sided term reproduces the ordering with a considerably larger negative TGR gap and a positive TE gap. The Rayleigh and truncated-normal variants returned point estimates without jackknife standard errors, and for those variants the TGR gap is close to zero or of the opposite sign; the truncated-normal variant returned a technology-gap estimate only. We draw no inference from them, and they mark the limit of the claim. The half-normal baseline is retained because it is the specification that estimates on every subsample and replicate, and the finding that credit users sit farther below the metafrontier is established under the half-normal and exponential distributions and under every treatment-definition, functional-form, estimator, aggregation, matching and regularity variant, but it is not established under every distributional assumption, and the paper does not claim otherwise. Taken together, the robustness exercise ranks the three findings by their stability: the negative technology gap is robust to the definition of credit, the functional form, the efficiency estimator, the aggregation rule, the matching scheme and the regularity restrictions; the negative MTE gap is robust in sign and moderately sensitive in magnitude; and the TE gap is small under every specification and its sign is not identified by these data.

## 5.6 Heterogeneity across financial-service use, farmers, crops and regions

The gaps reported so far average over households that differ in their other financial services, their characteristics, their crops and their locations. This subsection asks where the technology gap and the efficiency gap are concentrated. The disaggregated estimates summarize the operator-level TGR, TE and MTE from the single matched metafrontier within each subgroup; the frontiers are not re-estimated by subgroup, so the estimates describe heterogeneity within the main result rather than separate models, and the same associational reading applies. In Table 6 each cell is the credit-user mean less the non-user mean within the stated group.

Figure 2 and Table 6 examine the contrast across financial-service use, which is where the paper's framing in terms of financial inclusion rather than credit alone is tested; no exhibit reports the decomposition by the financial-inclusion index, which enters the analysis as a matching covariate rather than as a stratifier and whose construction is documented in Note S1. The technology gap is negative and significant within every financial-service subgroup the GLSS allows: `r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Has bank account/contributing to a scheme", 1), 1)` percentage points among households with a formal account, `r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Insured", 1), 1)` among the insured, and, across institution types, from `r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Mobile money", 1), 1)` points among mobile-money users to `r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Investment/mortgage", 1), 1)` among the small group holding an investment or mortgage account, with bank customers, savings-and-loans and susu scheme members and cooperative or credit-union members all in the same range. There is no financial-service configuration in the data within which borrowing households operate the best-practice technology, and holding another financial product does not narrow the technology gap of credit users. Where account ownership matters is on the efficiency margin. Figure 2 shows that among households without a formal account the TE contrast favours credit users and offsets most of the technology gap, so that the MTE gap is close to zero, whereas among account holders the TE contrast is negative and the MTE gap is clearly negative and at least as large as the aggregate gap of Table 4. The shortfall in meta-frontier efficiency associated with credit is therefore concentrated among the formally included, which is the opposite of the complementarity between credit and account ownership that the financial-inclusion literature anticipates [@Peprah2021; @DemirgucKunt2017]. Institution type matters in the same way: the TE contrast is strongly negative among susu-scheme participants (`r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Susu scheme", 2), 1)` points), whose MTE gap of `r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Susu scheme", 3), 1)` points is the largest among the institution types, and among customers of commercial, community and rural banks (`r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Commercial/community/rural bank", 2), 1)` points); it is indistinguishable from zero among mobile-money users; and it is positive among members of cooperatives and credit unions (`r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Cooperative/credit union", 2), 1)` points), for whom the efficiency advantage is large enough that credit users outperform matched non-users against the metafrontier by `r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Cooperative/credit union", 3), 1)` points. Membership-based institutions that combine credit with savings discipline and peer information are thus the one channel in which credit use coincides with better within-technology performance, in line with evidence that savings groups change household financial behaviour more than they change income [@Karlan2017], although the subgroup is small. The data cannot say whether these patterns reflect the kind of credit that account holders and scheme members obtain, the kind of household that holds an account, or the uses to which account-holding households put liquidity; read with the loan-purpose evidence of Table 3, they are consistent with borrowing among the formally included being directed to non-farm uses to a greater extent than borrowing among the unbanked, but the survey does not link loan purpose to the farm-level scores and this remains a conjecture. A decomposition of the credit contrast by the source of the loan and by its reported purpose, the two dimensions Table 3 records and that no current exhibit crosses with the operator-level scores, would test that conjecture directly; it is not available here, and we identify it as the cut the evidence most needs rather than anticipate what it would show. The source-of-information block of Table 6 is reported for completeness and not interpreted, because its category labels do not map consistently onto the corresponding block of Table 2 read in Section 3, and the reasons-for-no-account block, whose category indicators rest on the same response-coding mechanism, is likewise left uninterpreted.

Figure 3 disaggregates by operator gender, age and education. The technology gap is negative and significant in every group, so no demographic group of credit users operates a technology closer to best practice than its matched non-users. The gap is wider for female than for male operators, which is consistent with the larger technology gap for female-operated farms in Table S4 and with the gender gaps in technology use documented on the same data [@Adaku2023]; it narrows steadily with operator age; and it is not monotone in schooling, being smallest for operators with no formal education and larger at every level of schooling. The efficiency contrast is small, within about two percentage points, for every group but one: it favours credit users among female operators, operators under sixty and those with no formal, primary or senior secondary schooling, is negligible for men, runs against credit users for the oldest operators, and is strongly negative for the small group educated beyond senior secondary level, for whom credit users are markedly less efficient within their own technology. The MTE gap is negative in every group, smallest for operators with senior secondary schooling and with no formal education, where an efficiency advantage offsets part of the technology gap, and largest by a wide margin for the post-secondary group, where the two margins compound. The expectation that better-educated, prime-age male operators would convert credit into technology gains more readily is not borne out; the technology gap is broad-based, and where the credit contrast is least adverse it is because of an efficiency offset, not a smaller technology gap.

Figure 4 disaggregates by major crop and by administrative region. Across crops the technology gap is negative for nine of the eleven crops shown, largest for pepper, maize, cassava and rice and smallest for millet, plantain and yam; it is indistinguishable from zero for sorghum and positive, though small, only for cocoa, the one crop for which credit-using households operate a technology closer to best practice than their matched non-users. The cocoa exception is consistent with the large cocoa-share coefficient in the credit-user frontier noted in Section 5.2, and cocoa is also the one export crop, with sector-specific input and extension arrangements of its own [@Tsiboe2016], but whether the exception reflects those arrangements or the selection of better-endowed households into cocoa borrowing cannot be established from the survey, which does not record loan purpose by crop. The efficiency contrasts by crop are small and of mixed sign, favouring credit users for plantain, groundnut, maize, rice and cassava, running against them for pepper, cocoa and yam, and not significant for millet, beans and sorghum, so the MTE gap is negative for most crops, widest for pepper, rice, millet, beans and maize, indistinguishable from zero for sorghum and cocoa, and positive only for plantain, where a large efficiency advantage outweighs a moderate technology gap. Across regions the technology gap is negative in all ten, widest in Volta and Greater Accra and narrowest in Northern and Western regions; the efficiency contrast is essentially zero in the three northern regions and in Greater Accra, favours credit users in Volta, Central and Eastern, and runs against them in Brong Ahafo, Ashanti and Western; and the MTE gap is negative in every region except Eastern, where it is not significant, and largest in Upper East. The crop and regional patterns do not sort neatly by agro-ecology or by cash-crop status, since the smallest and among the largest technology gaps are both in southern regions, and they do not line up with the density of financial services in Table 2, so we do not attempt to attribute them. What they establish is that the technology gap is pervasive rather than concentrated in a few systems, while the efficiency contrast varies in sign from one setting to another, which is more consistent with readings that operate through the household, such as loan use and selection, than with one that operates through the lending environment.

For targeting, the heterogeneity results cut two ways. Because the technology gap is negative in nearly every subgroup, there is no identifiable class of borrowers, defined by service use, gender, age, schooling, crop or region, for whom credit use is associated with a technology closer to best practice; cocoa producers and, on the efficiency margin, cooperative and credit-union members are the nearest to exceptions. Where the subgroups differ is in whether credit users make up part of the technology gap through better within-technology performance, as unbanked households, younger and female operators and plantain and groundnut producers do, or compound it, as banked households, the most educated operators and susu participants do. That is a statement about where managerial support would and would not find a deficit to close, and about the fact that the subgroups in which the overall shortfall is largest, account holders and the post-secondary educated, are not those a financial-inclusion programme would ordinarily prioritize; it is not evidence that credit itself works better for some groups than for others.
